Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 75, verses 1–6:

﴿Nay, I swear﴾: In both places, its meaning is "I swear" (aqsimu). The *la* (لا) is extra, added to emphasize the oath. It is also said that it is an opening of speech, equivalent to *ala* (ألا, "verily"). It is also said that it is a negation of the disbelievers' statement. ﴿by the self-reproaching soul﴾: It is the one that blames itself for committing sins or falling short in acts of obedience. The souls are of three kinds: the best is the tranquil soul (al-nafs al-mutma'innah), the worst is the soul that commands evil (al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su'), and between them is the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah). It is also said that the *lawwamah* is the blameworthy, wicked one, but this is far-fetched, because God swears only by created things that are great, and it works if *la* in "lā uqsimu" is a negation of the oath.

﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾: *Al-insan* (the human being) here refers to the species, or the reference is to the disbelievers who deny the resurrection. Its meaning is: does he suppose that We will not gather his bones for resurrection after they have decayed into dust? This sentence is what indicates the answer to the oath mentioned above. ﴿Yes﴾: its implied meaning is "We will gather them." ﴿Man﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *najma'u* (we gather), and the meaning is: We gather them while We are able. ﴿That We will not assemble his bones﴾: *Al-banān* means the fingers. There are two opinions on its meaning. One is that it is a statement about the power to resurrect, meaning: We are able to make his fingers even, that is, to create them again after their annihilation, perfectly formed and precise. The fingers are singled out from the other limbs because their bones are fine and separate. The other is that it is a threat in this world, meaning: We are able to make his fingers even, joined together like the hoof of a donkey or the sole of a camel, so that he cannot manipulate his hands for his benefits. The first is more fitting to the context of the speech.

﴿But man desires to continue in sin before him﴾: This sentence is conjoined to "does man think". It may be interrogative like it, or it may be declarative. *Bal* here is not for retraction (idrab, انصراف) from the first statement in the sense of nullifying it; rather, it is for moving away from it to what follows. *Li-yafjura* means that he may perform acts of wickedness. There are three opinions on the meaning of *amamahu* (before him). One is that it is an expression for the time that lies ahead, meaning that he will act wickedly for the rest of his life. The second is that it is an expression for following his desires and appetites; it is said: "So-and-so walked ahead of him" when he does not turn back from something he wants. The pronoun in these two opinions refers to man. The third is that the pronoun refers to the Day of Resurrection, and the meaning is: man desires to commit wickedness before the Day of Resurrection.

﴿He asks: when is the Day of Resurrection?﴾: *Ayyan* means "when". This question about the Day of Resurrection is asked in a manner of mockery and derision.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 75, verses 7–9:

﴿So the sight will be dazzled﴾. This is an announcement about the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said that it refers to the state of death, but this is an error, because the moon does not eclipse at the death of anyone, nor is it joined with the sun. "Baraqa" with a fatha on the ra' means it shone and acquired a glare (barq). It is also read with a kasra on the ra', and its meaning is that it was bewildered from fright. It has also been said that its meaning is that it stared fixedly, so the meanings of the fatha and the kasra come close together. ﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾: its light has gone. It is said: "khasafa huwa" and "khasafahu Allah," and khusuf is used for the moon and kusuf for the sun. It has also been said that kusuf is the going of part of the light, and khusuf is the going of all of it, and it has also been said that they have the same meaning. ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined together﴾: regarding their joining there are three opinions. The first is that they are joined where God makes them rise from the west. The second is that they are joined on the Day of Resurrection, and then they are cast into the Fire, and it has been said into the sea, so that they become the Great Fire. The third is that they are joined and their light is thereby lost.

﴿No refuge!﴾ That is, there is no place of safety and no one to help.

﴿With what he sent forward and left behind﴾: that is, with all his deeds; what he sent forward of them at the beginning of his life, and what he left behind at its end. It is said: what he advanced during his lifetime, and what he left behind after his death, such as a tradition (sunnah) or a bequest (wasiyyah). It is also said: what he sent forward for himself of his wealth, and what he left of it for his heirs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 75, verses 14–15:

﴿Nay, man will be a witness against himself﴾ Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first: he is a witness against himself through his deeds, for his limbs will testify against him on the Day of Resurrection. The second: he is a clear proof, because his own creation points to his Creator, and so he is described as having insight (baṣīrah) metaphorically, since whoever reflects upon himself perceives the truth. The first is more fitting with what precedes and follows it, as if He said: "Man will be informed on that Day of his deeds; nay, he is a witness against his deeds even if he is not informed of them." It also coheres with His words: ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾, and the answer to "even if" (law) is what we shall mention, according to this reading. ﴿Even if he presents his excuses﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: al-ma'ādhīr means the excuses; that is, man testifies against himself by his deeds even if he offers excuses for their ugliness. The second: al-ma'ādhīr means the veils (al-sutūr); that is, man testifies against himself on the Day of Resurrection even if he drew veils over himself in the world when he committed the ugly deeds.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 75, verses 16–19:

﴿Do not move your tongue with it, to hasten it.﴾ The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) refers to the Qur'an, as the context of the situation indicates. The occasion of the revelation of this verse is that when Jibril came down to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with the Qur'an, he would move his lips with it, fearing that he would forget it immediately. So Allah commanded him to be silent and listen. It was also said: he feared forgetting the Qur'an, so he would recite it repeatedly until this became burdensome for him and difficult upon him, and then this verse was revealed. The first view is the sound one, because it is related in al-Bukhari and others. ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ Allah guaranteed to him that He would gather it in his breast, so he would not need to move his lips when it was revealed. The word "qur'anahu" here may bear two meanings. One: that it means recitation (qira'ah), since al-Qur'an may be a verbal noun from "qara'tu" (I recited). The other: that it means its composition in his breast, being a verbal noun from your saying "qara'tu al-shay'" (I gathered the thing). ﴿So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation.﴾ That is, when Jibril recites it, then make Jibril's recitation the recitation of Allah, since it is from Him. The meaning of "follow its recitation" is: listen to its recitation and follow it with your mind so that you may memorize it. It was also said: follow the Qur'an in its commands and prohibitions. ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation.﴾ That is, it is upon Us to explain it to you and to make you memorize it. It was also said: it is upon Us to explain its meanings and rulings. If it is asked: what is the connection of His saying, ﴿Do not move your tongue with it﴾ and what follows, to what precedes it? The answer: perhaps it was revealed together with it at one time, so it was placed in the order of revelation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 75, verse 20:

﴿Nay, but you love the hasty life (al-ʿājilah)﴾, that is, you love the worldly life. This address is a rebuke to the disbelievers, and to whoever is in the same state as them in loving the world. And "kallā" is a deterrent from that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 75, verses 22–25:

﴿Some faces that Day will be radiant﴾ — with the letter ḍād, meaning bright and blessed (nā‘ima), and from it comes ﴿the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24]. ﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾ — this is from seeing with the eye, and it is a textual proof for the believers' seeing of Allah Most High in the Hereafter. This is the position of the Ahl al-Sunnah. The Mu'tazilah denied it and interpreted nāẓirah to mean "awaiting" (muntaẓirah), but this is invalid, because naẓara in the sense of intaẓara (to wait for) takes its object without a preposition: you say naẓartuka, meaning "I waited for you." As for the verb governed by ilā (to), it is from seeing with the eye, as in His saying: ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ [Yunus: 43]. Some of them said that ilā here is not a preposition but is the plural of ālā'  (bounties), meaning blessings; but this is a far-fetched strain in the extreme. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it to mean the same as people's saying: "So-and-so looks to so-and-so" when he hopes for him and depends on him; but this is remote. Sound and widely transmitted hadiths have come from the Prophet ﷺ about seeing Allah, clear in meaning and not admitting of interpretation, and they are the explanation of the verse.

﴿Scowling﴾ — frowning, on which sadness is visible; al-busur is stronger than al-subus (frowning). ﴿Thinking that a calamity will be inflicted upon them﴾ — a catastrophe that breaks the back. The word "thinking" (ẓann) here may be in its original sense, or it may mean certainty (yaqīn).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 75, verses 26–30:

﴿When it reaches the collarbones﴾: he means the state of death. Al-tarāqī (the collarbones) is the plural of tarqūwah, which are the bones at the top of the chest. The subject of "balaghat" (reached) is the soul of the person, as the context of the speech indicates. It refers to the state of ḥashrajah (the rattle in the throat) and the agony of death. ﴿And it is said, "Who can heal?"﴾: that is, the people of the sick man say, "Who will perform ruqyah (spiritual healing recitation) for him, perhaps he will be cured?" It is also said that the meaning is that the angels say, "Who will ascend with his soul," that is, carry it up to heaven? The first is from ruqyah, and it is more well-known and apparent, while the second is from ruqiyy, which means ascent. ﴿And he thinks it is the parting﴾: that is, the sick man is certain that this state is the parting from the world, from his family and from his wealth. ﴿And leg is wound about leg﴾: this is an expression of the severity of the distress of death and its agonies, that is, his leg is wrapped around the other at the time of the final agony. It is also said that it is a majāz (metaphor), like the saying "the war uncovered its leg," when it intensifies. It is also said that the meaning is that his leg has died so it cannot carry him. And it is said: "iltaffat" means the disbeliever wrapped it up, if he disbelieved. In His saying "al-sāq" (the leg) and "al-masāq" (the driving) there is a kind of tajnīs (a figure of speech based on paronomasia). ﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the driving﴾: this is the answer to "when it reaches the collarbones." Al-masāq is a verbal noun from "sawq" (driving), as in His saying: ﴿And to Allah is the destination﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 28].

Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on verses 31–35 of surah 75:

﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ Here "lā" is negating (lā nāfiyah), and "ṣaddaqa" here may mean either belief in God and His messengers (taṣdīq) or giving charity (ṣadaqah). This verse and what follows were revealed concerning Abu Jahl. ﴿He went swaggering to his family﴾ That is, he walked with a conceited, strutting gait, which is an expression of arrogance and self-importance. This manner of walking was well known among the Banu Makhzum, of whom Abu Jahl was one. ﴿Woe to you, and woe⁠—﴾ This is a threat and a warning. ﴿Then woe to you, and woe⁠—﴾ This is a second threat, and it was repeated for emphasis. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seized Abu Jahl by the collar of his garment and said to him: "Indeed Allah says to you: Woe to you, and woe! Then woe to you, and woe!" Then the Qur'an was revealed in agreement with that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 75, verses 36–40:

﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾ This is a rebuke, and its meaning is: does he suppose that he will be left without resurrection, without reckoning, and without recompense? It is like His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. Here "al-insan" (man) is a generic noun, and it has been said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It is not far-fetched that its occasion of revelation was specific while its meaning is general. ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ The nutfah (drop) is a small quantity of fluid, and tumna is from your saying: amná al-rajul (the man ejaculated). The meaning of the verse is: an argument from the creation of man for his resurrection, like His saying: ﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time﴾ [Ya-Sin: 79].
